_readme: The alarm keyword vocabulary, shared VERBATIM by kp-front and kp-rueck.
WHAT IS IN HERE, AND WHOSE IT IS. German fire-service alarm words (FEUER, VU, MED USTÜ)
routed onto the Swiss FKS damage categories. Nothing below belongs to an alerting vendor:
the words are the fire service's and the categories are the canton's. Divera is how these
words reach the station that wrote this file first — the delivery, not the definition. It
was called divera_keywords.json until 2026-08-02 and was renamed for that reason, the same
reason `divera_id` gave way to `source`/`source_ref` on the incident: naming a shared thing
after one deployment's provider makes it look like a Divera feature to everybody else.
IT IS A DEFAULT, NOT A CONSTANT. A station whose alarm vocabulary differs — another
language, another Stichwort set, another alerting system — sets `alarmKeywords` in its
deployment config (kp-front: docs/CONFIGURATION.md §1a) and that block REPLACES this file
wholesale for that deployment. There is no per-keyword merging: a station that sets it owns
the entire vocabulary, because at 3am «which keywords are running» must have one answer in
one place. Wanting one extra keyword therefore means copying this file and adding to the
copy. This file stays the shipped default, stays vendored into both products and stays
pinned by checksum; a deployment's own vocabulary is deployment data and is compared
against nothing.
WHY A FILE. Both products read the same dispatch system and had independently grown the
same two tables: 19 title keywords routed to the same eleven damage categories, and 41
priority keywords in the same order. Two hand-maintained copies of one vocabulary, and
nothing compared them - a keyword added on one side simply did not exist on the other.
WHY NOT A LIBRARY. kp-front and kp-rueck ship separate databases, separate images and
separate releases, and docs/RUNNING-BOTH.md promises self-hosters no shared library and no
runtime coupling. Neither may import the other. So the copies stay copies and a test
compares them: this file is vendored byte-for-byte into both repositories and pinned by
checksum, exactly like app/telemetry/. Editing it is a two-repository change.
MATCHING IS NOT IN HERE, ON PURPOSE. This file is a vocabulary, not an algorithm. Each
product keeps its own matcher and they are NOT identical today: kp-rueck requires letter
boundaries for GAS, VU and LIFT so 'GAS' does not fire on 'GASSE', while kp-front matches
every keyword as a plain substring. That difference is real, it changes which alarms come
out HIGH, and converging it is a product decision about the alarm path rather than a
housekeeping one - so it is recorded here as a known divergence instead of being quietly
settled by whoever edited this file last.
LABELS ARE NOT IN HERE EITHER. The categories below are stable keys. What an operator
reads is each product's own vocabulary: kp-front stores a German display string on the
incident, kp-rueck stores the key and translates in the frontend. They also disagree -
'BMA / unechte Alarme' vs 'BMA / Unechte Alarme'. One of those is a stored value in a
released product, so the disagreement is left alone and named rather than migrated. It is
also why the category keys are not free-form: a deployment's own vocabulary must route to
categories the product has a label for, and is rejected at load if it does not.
NOT IN SCOPE. Vehicle, group and RIC aliases are deliberately absent. They are not shared
between these two products - kp-front reads its fleet and groups from the deployment
config, kp-rueck's vehicle rows are development fixtures - and the real alias problem
spans WinFAP, Traccar and Divera, which are not these repositories. When the stable slot
key lands, it should EXTEND this file rather than replace it: same mechanism, same test.
Alarm title keyword -> damage category key. ORDER MATTERS: the matcher walks this list
and the first keyword found in the uppercased title wins. Keys are uppercase and
compared against an uppercased title. Nothing matched falls through to fallback_category.
Any match anywhere in title + text makes the alarm HIGH; everything else is LOW. Order is
irrelevant here (it is an any-match, not a first-hit), so the grouping below is for the
reader. Only life-threatening situations belong in this list - it is not a severity
ranking, it is the answer to 'wake everyone up'.

groups.note: Specific phrases, not the bare word 'PERSON': 'PERSON IN' covers Person in Lift and Person in Gefahr, 'PERSON IM' covers Person im Wasser. 'ABSTURZ' covers Person abgestürzt.
GASLECK is listed even though it contains GAS, because a matcher that requires letter boundaries for GAS would otherwise miss it.
'MED USTÜ' is Medizinische Unterstützung, 'MED.' is Med. Notfall - the trailing dot keeps it off words starting with 'med'.

_readme: Recorded so it stays a decision. kp-rueck matches these three with letter boundaries
((?<![A-ZÄÖÜ])KW(?![A-ZÄÖÜ])); kp-front matches them as plain substrings. Neither is
unambiguously right: boundaries stop 'GAS' firing on 'GASSE', and also stop it firing on
'GASFLASCHE'. Listed as data so a future convergence has something to point at.
